**Who chooses the tool?** The model. It reads each tool's description and picks one; the MCP client only carries the request and the result. *(On the exam: tool descriptions drive tool selection, TS 2.1.)*

**Two agents.** A research agent chose and called the tools. A synthesis agent with no tools then wrote the answer and chose any chart from the question and the tool results alone. *(On the exam: a subagent's context is passed in, not inherited, TS 1.3.)*
**Was the result changed?** No. The tables printed the values the tool returned; the untouched JSON was under Details.
**The model** was Gemini; the Claude terms were shown beside it. No API key was passed to a server.

tools.name: get_hardware_spec
tools.summary: Describe this computer's hardware and operating system: maker and model, processor name, physical and logical core counts, total and currently available memory (RAM) in GB, graphics adapters, battery charge if it has a battery, and the Windows version.
tools.full:
Describe this computer's hardware and operating system: maker and model, processor name, physical
and logical core counts, total and currently available memory (RAM) in GB, graphics adapters, battery
charge if it has a battery, and the Windows version.

Takes no input. Use it for questions like "what laptop is this?", "how much RAM do I have?" or
"is this machine good enough for X?".
It does NOT report disk space (use get_storage), which folders are large (use get_folder_sizes) or
which programs are using memory right now (use get_top_processes).
It never returns the computer name, user name, serial numbers or network addresses.

tools.name: get_storage
tools.summary: Report how full each disk drive on this computer is: total size, space used, space free (in GB) and the percentage used, one row per drive.
tools.full:
Report how full each disk drive on this computer is: total size, space used, space free (in GB) and
the percentage used, one row per drive.

Takes no input. Use it for "how much disk space is left?" or "which drive is nearly full?".
It reports whole drives only. To see WHICH folders take the space use get_folder_sizes; for WHAT KIND of
files use summarize_file_types; to project when a drive fills up use estimate_disk_runway.

tools.name: get_folder_sizes
tools.summary: List the folders directly inside one folder with the size of each (GB) and its file count, largest first.
tools.full:
List the folders directly inside one folder with the size of each (GB) and its file count, largest
first. Use it to find WHICH folders take up disk space.

Input: `path` — a folder inside your home folder, either absolute ("C:\Users\you\Downloads") or
relative to home ("Downloads", "Documents\Projects"). Leave it empty for the home folder itself.
Example questions: "what's using the space in my Downloads folder?", "which of my folders is biggest?".

Limits: only folders inside the home folder are allowed (anything else is refused); it returns names
and sizes, never file contents; counting stops after about 8 seconds, and `complete` is then false with
the sizes counted so far. For whole-drive totals use get_storage; for a breakdown by kind of file
(documents, images, video…) use summarize_file_types.

tools.name: summarize_file_types
tools.summary: Break a folder's contents down by KIND of file — documents, images, video, audio, archives and installers, code, other — with the total size (GB) and file count of each kind, largest first.
tools.full:
Break a folder's contents down by KIND of file — documents, images, video, audio, archives and
installers, code, other — with the total size (GB) and file count of each kind, largest first.

Input: `path` — a folder inside your home folder (absolute, or relative to home such as "Downloads").
Leave it empty for the whole home folder.
Use it for "what kind of files fill my Downloads?" or "how much of my space is video?".
It returns totals per kind only: no file or folder names. Counting stops after about 8 seconds and
`complete` is then false. For sizes per folder use get_folder_sizes instead.

tools.name: get_top_processes
tools.summary: List the programs currently using the most memory or processor time on this computer: program name, memory in MB, processor seconds used so far, and how many copies are running.
tools.full:
List the programs currently using the most memory or processor time on this computer: program name,
memory in MB, processor seconds used so far, and how many copies are running.

Input: `by` — "memory" (default) or "cpu". `limit` — 1 to 20, default 8.
Use it for "what is using my memory?", "why is my laptop slow right now?".
It reports what is running NOW. For the computer's total and free memory use get_hardware_spec.
It returns program names only: no window titles, file paths or user names.

tools.name: estimate_disk_runway
tools.summary: Project when a drive will be full if it keeps filling at a steady rate.
tools.full:
Project when a drive will be full if it keeps filling at a steady rate. Returns the days left until
full, the date it would fill up, and the expected used space (GB) today and after 30, 90, 180 and 365
days.

Input: `daily_growth_gb` — GB added per day, e.g. 0.5 (must be above 0). `drive` — the drive letter,
default "C".
Use it for "how long until my disk is full if I add 2 GB a day?". It is arithmetic on today's free
space: a projection, not a measurement. For today's figures alone use get_storage.

tools.name: check_internet
tools.summary: Test whether this computer can reach the internet right now, and how quickly: it opens a connection to three well-known websites and reports, for each, whether it worked and the time taken in ms.
tools.full:
Test whether this computer can reach the internet right now, and how quickly: it opens a connection
to three well-known websites and reports, for each, whether it worked and the time taken in ms.

Takes no input. Use it for "am I online?", "is my connection slow?" or before blaming a website.
It does not measure download speed and returns no network addresses. To look something up on the web
use web_search.

tools.name: web_search
tools.summary: Search the public web and return the top results: title, URL and a short snippet for each.
tools.full:
Search the public web and return the top results: title, URL and a short snippet for each.

Input: `query` — plain search words, e.g. "Intel Core i7-1165G7 release date" or "Windows 11 minimum
RAM". `max_results` — 1 to 10, default 5.
Use it for facts that are NOT on this computer: product details, prices, release dates, how-to pages.
Do not use it for this computer's own hardware, disk space or running programs — the other tools answer
those directly — or to test the connection (use check_internet).

It returns search-result snippets, not full pages, and the text comes from third-party websites, so
treat it as unverified. No results is a valid answer (count is 0), not an error.

tools.name: save_note
tools.summary: Save a short note to this computer's notes file, with today's date.
tools.full:
Save a short note to this computer's notes file, with today's date. The ONLY tool here that changes
anything. Before writing, the server asks the user to confirm; if the user declines, nothing is saved.

Input: `text` — the note, up to 500 characters, e.g. "Cleared Downloads on 4 Oct, freed 12 GB".
Use it only when the user asks to remember, record or note something down. The saved notes can be read

laptop://policy/cleanup.text:
# Laptop clean-up policy (MOCK - example data for learning)

1. Never delete from a folder marked `safe_to_clear = no` in the folder catalog.
2. A folder marked `review` needs a person to look at the files first.
3. Keep at least 15% of a drive free. Below that, plan a clean-up.
4. Clear `Temp` first, then `Downloads` items older than their keep_days.
5. Rebuildable folders (for example `.venv`) may be deleted to free space.
6. Write down what was cleared, and when, with the save_note tool.

serverRules.heading: What a server author controls (laptop_server.py)
rules: **Descriptions.** The description of each tool is the only thing a model reads when it chooses (guide TS 2.1). Each says what the tool returns, its input, and when to use a different tool.

**Failures are failures.** `fail()` raises, the SDK sets `isError: true`, and the message carries `errorCategory`, `isRetryable` and a plain explanation (guide TS 2.2). An empty result is not an error: an empty search is a valid result (`count` is 0).
**Resources give a catalogue up front**, so the agent does not have to explore with tool calls (guide TS 2.4).

**The server decides what it will NOT reveal.** No tool returns the computer name, user name, serial numbers, network addresses or file contents, and file-system tools are limited to the home folder. Whatever a tool does return is sent to the model, so treat every field as leaving the machine.
**Time budget.** `get_folder_sizes` and `summarize_file_types` stop counting after about 8 seconds and say so (`complete` is false).

**Elicitation.** `save_note` is the only tool that changes anything. It asks the user to confirm before writing; if the user declines, nothing is saved. On the original page a web form could not pause mid-call, so the Decline / Approve choice was a pre-set answer.
**Notifications.** Progress and log messages are sent while `get_folder_sizes` and `summarize_file_types` run. They were shown to the user and never sent to the model.
serverRules.hostedWho: **What is whose on the hosted server.** The 21 tools are the community `sec-edgar-mcp` package's, registered unchanged (AGPL-3.0, not written or endorsed by the SEC, per its README). The resources and prompts were added by this workbench so every MCP server feature could be shown; the upstream package ships none.
serverRules.hostedWhy: **Why the ticker list matters** (guide TS 2.4: a resource is a catalogue that saves exploratory tool calls). In live runs the package's `search_companies` tool returned nothing for well-known names, so the model fell back on tickers it remembered. With `edgar://tickers` attached, the name to ticker to CIK step is read from data instead of guessed.

rules.fact: None. The SEC page states: “These APIs do not require any authentication or API keys to access.”
The SEC asks for no more than 10 requests per second per user. The library this server uses throttles itself to 8 per second (`max_requests_per_second = 8`).

Each request carries a `User-Agent` header with the text of `SEC_EDGAR_USER_AGENT` (`headers["User-Agent"] = identity`). The SEC developer page says it does not allow automated tools that identify themselves as unclassified bots.

None described. The SEC pages list RESTful JSON APIs, RSS feeds, index files, daily archives and an HTTPS file system; no SQL or query interface is mentioned. In my 44 logged requests, none had a query string (nothing after a `?`).
`data.sec.gov` does not support CORS, so a browser page cannot call it directly. A program on a server — like this MCP server — makes the call instead.
The data APIs return JSON. A filing is a text file.

hops.what: The agent sends the question and all the tools' names, descriptions and input schemas to Gemini
hops.sent: Gemini answers with a **function call**: a tool name plus arguments, as JSON. It is a choice of tool, not a query

hops.what: The MCP client sends that call to the MCP server
hops.over: HTTP POST to `http://127.0.0.1:9870/mcp` — a JSON-RPC message with `method: tools/call`; it never leaves this machine
hops.sent: `name` and `arguments`, copied from the function call

hops.what: The tool runs. It is an ordinary Python function in the server process
hops.over: HTTPS GET to `data.sec.gov` and `www.sec.gov` — the only step that goes to the SEC
hops.sent: It builds URLs from the CIK or accession number. Filtering and parsing happen in Python, on the JSON or text that came back

tools.question: What is Apple's CIK?
tools.code:
def get_cik_by_ticker(ticker="AAPL"):                 # sec_edgar_mcp/utils/cache.py
    if ticker_cache is empty:                         # only the FIRST call in a server process
        GET https://www.sec.gov/files/company_tickers_exchange.json
            # a static JSON file: a list of [cik, name, ticker, exchange]
        ticker_cache = { ticker: cik  for each row in the file }
    cik = ticker_cache.get("AAPL")                    # a dictionary lookup in memory: no SEC call
    return {"success": True, "cik": zero_pad(cik, 10), "ticker": "AAPL"}
tools.note: The second call made no request at all: the ticker list is kept in memory for the life of the server process.

tools.question: List the two most recent 10-K filings for Apple.
tools.code:
def get_recent_filings(identifier="AAPL", form_type="10-K", days=30, limit=2):
    company = get_company(identifier)                 # ticker -> CIK (see get_cik_by_ticker), then edgartools Company(cik)
    filings = company.get_filings(form="10-K")
        GET https://data.sec.gov/submissions/CIK0000320193.json
            # REST: the company's details and its recent filings, as JSON
        GET https://data.sec.gov/submissions/CIK0000320193-submissions-001.json
            # older filings; the first file names these extra files (edgartools entity/data.py)
        # "10-K only" is applied in Python on the downloaded list: no query string is sent
    rows = []
    for filing in filings:                            # newest first
        if len(rows) >= limit: break
        rows.append({accession_number, filing_date, form, company, cik, period_of_report})
        # observed: one more GET of  /Archives/edgar/data/320193/<accession>.txt  per filing returned
        # (why edgartools fetches that file was not checked)
    return {"success": True, "filings": rows, "count": len(rows)}
tools.note: The `days` argument is accepted but never used: in the code it appears only in the function's signature.

tools.question: What was Apple's revenue and net income in its latest filing?
tools.code:
def get_financials(identifier="AAPL", statement_type="income"):    # sec_edgar_mcp/tools/financial.py
    company = get_company(identifier)
    latest_10k = company.get_filings(form="10-K").latest()    # the two submissions files, as above
    latest_10q = company.get_filings(form="10-Q").latest()
    latest = whichever has the LATER filing_date              # so "latest" can be a quarterly 10-Q
    financials = Financials.extract(latest)
        GET https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/320193/000032019326000020/0000320193-26-000020.txt
            # the whole filing as one text file; it contains the XBRL data
            # (the folder name is the accession number without its dashes)
            # observed: this file was fetched twice
    income = financials.income_statement()                    # parsed from that XBRL, in Python
    return {"success": True, "statements": {"income_statement": income},
            "filing_reference": {accession_number, filing_date, form_type, sec_url}}
tools.note: No XBRL query was sent to the SEC: the numbers were read out of the filing text after it arrived.

tools.question: Give me Apple's key figures from its company facts.
tools.code:
def get_company_facts(identifier="AAPL"):                 # tools/company.py
    company = get_company(identifier)
    facts = company.get_facts()
        GET https://data.sec.gov/api/xbrl/companyfacts/CIK0000320193.json
            # REST: every XBRL fact the company has reported, as one JSON file
    metrics = {}
    if hasattr(facts, "data"):                            # <- the tool only looks inside facts.data
        for name in [Assets, Liabilities, StockholdersEquity, Revenues, NetIncomeLoss,
                     EarningsPerShareBasic, CashAndCashEquivalents, CommonStockSharesOutstanding]:
            if name in facts.data["us-gaap"]: metrics[name] = the latest value
    return {"success": True, "metrics": metrics, "has_facts": True}
tools.note: This one returned `"metrics": {}` with `success: true` for Apple. The SEC file arrived (HTTP 200), but the installed edgartools returns an `EntityFacts` object that has no `.data` attribute, so the tool's loop never ran. An empty result that looks like success: the case the exam asks you to tell apart from a failure (TS 2.2).
